title: The Running Tab Between You and the Business That Nobody Reconciles
excerpt: Money moves quietly between owner and business in almost every SME, covering a gap here, absorbing a personal cost there. Left informal, that balance turns into a problem at exactly the wrong moment.
content:
In most owner-led businesses, the first entry in a loan account is nothing dramatic. Trade is tight one month, so the owner transfers a few thousand dollars from a personal account to cover payroll or a supplier payment. Nobody thinks of it as a loan. It felt like the responsible thing to do.

Then the pattern runs the other way. The business covers something that is really a personal cost, a family holiday on the company card, a dividend drawn against a profit result that has not been confirmed yet, a bonus timed around what the bank balance can absorb rather than what the year actually delivered. Each entry makes sense on its own. None of them were ever meant to be permanent.

Years later, the balance is real money, moving in both directions, with no interest rate, no repayment schedule, and no one who owns the decision about what happens to it. It sits quietly on the balance sheet as a loan account, correctly recorded, rarely discussed, until someone outside the business needs it explained.

How the balance builds without anyone deciding it should

None of this happens through carelessness. Your bookkeeper or BAS agent is doing exactly what they should be doing, recording each transaction accurately as it happens and keeping the loan account balance correct in the ledger. What compliance accounting is not designed to do is ask whether that balance should exist in its current form, or whether the business and the owner should be treating it as the facility it has effectively become. That is a commercial question, not a bookkeeping one, and in most owner-led businesses nobody is asking it.

The result is a balance that grows or shrinks based on cash flow convenience rather than any deliberate decision. A strong quarter pulls it back toward zero. A tight one pushes it out again. Over a few years the swings smooth out and the balance settles into a habit, a standing arrangement that nobody signed off on and nobody reviews.

Why it looks fine until someone else has to make sense of it

An informal loan account rarely causes a problem on its own. It becomes a problem the moment someone outside the business has to interpret it. A bank assessing serviceability for a new facility wants to know whether that balance is money the business can call on or a liability sitting against it, and an undocumented answer reads as risk rather than strength. A buyer working through the early stages of a business valuation will ask the same question with less patience, because a loan account with no terms is one more item that has to be unwound or explained before a price can be agreed. The ATO also takes a specific interest in director and shareholder loan balances that run for extended periods without documented terms, which is worth raising with your compliance accountant well before it becomes an issue rather than after.

None of this means the arrangement was wrong to begin with. Owners support their businesses through tight months constantly, and the reverse happens just as often. The issue is not that the money moved. It is that it was never converted into something with terms, so it carries the shape of a problem even when it is not one.

Treating it like the facility it actually is

The fix is smaller than it sounds. A loan account becomes low risk the moment it has the basic structure of any other facility, an agreed interest rate, even a modest one, a repayment schedule or at least a ceiling it is not allowed to exceed, and a documented resolution that records why it exists. None of that requires unwinding the arrangement or the owner repaying everything at once. It requires deciding, on purpose, what the arrangement actually is.

This is the kind of gap a banking and facility review is built to catch, because it looks at every source of funding running through a business, not only the ones with a bank's name on them. For businesses working on broader cash flow discipline, formalising the loan account is usually a half-day conversation, not a project.

Most owners already sense which side of this their business sits on. If the honest answer is that nobody could explain the loan account balance on request, that is worth fixing before a bank, a buyer, or the ATO asks the question first. A fractional CFO relationship exists partly for gaps exactly this size, small enough to fix in an afternoon, large enough to matter the day someone else looks closely.

faqs.q: What is a director's loan account and why does almost every SME have one?
faqs.a: It is the running balance of money that has moved between an owner and their business outside normal wages or dividends, an owner covering a shortfall one month, the business covering a personal cost the next. It shows up because owner-led businesses naturally absorb each other's cash gaps, not because anything has gone wrong.

faqs.q: Does a director's loan account legally need to be repaid to the business?
faqs.a: In most structures, yes, money owed to the business by a director is expected to be repaid or formally documented as a dividend or wage, rather than left open-ended indefinitely. The specific rules depend heavily on your business structure and the timing involved, which makes it a conversation worth having directly and early with your compliance accountant.

faqs.q: Why does the ATO pay attention to loans between a business and its owner?
faqs.a: Extended, undocumented balances between a company and its director can be treated differently to an ordinary business debt, particularly around how they are taxed if the balance is left unresolved for too long. We are not tax advisers, so this is one worth raising early with your BAS agent or compliance accountant, rather than after the fact.

faqs.q: Can an unclear loan account reduce how much a bank will lend my business?
faqs.a: Yes. Lenders assessing serviceability want a clean read on what is genuine business debt versus money owed to or from the owner, and an undocumented balance often gets treated as a risk by default. A banking and facility review looks at exactly this kind of gap before a lender does.

faqs.q: Will a buyer care about a director's loan account when I sell my business?
faqs.a: Almost always. An outstanding loan account is one of the first things a buyer's advisor flags during due diligence, because it has to be settled or explained before a price is agreed. Cleaning it up early, well before a sale conversation starts, is a small but genuine part of broader exit readiness work.

faqs.q: How can a fractional CFO help formalise a loan account between an owner and the business?
faqs.a: Part of the role is spotting structural gaps like this before they become urgent, then setting terms, an interest rate, and regular review points so the balance stops drifting on its own. If you have not worked with one before, this guide on what a fractional CFO does is a useful starting point.
